title: Zero Pivot: PA = LU with a Row Exchange
quickIdea: When the next pivot is zero, swap in a row from below; the swap is recorded in a permutation matrix P, and the factorization becomes PA = LU.
remember: A permutation matrix P has exactly one 1 in each row and column; it is orthogonal, so P^T P = I, and det(P) is +1 or -1 according to the parity of the swaps.
Partial pivoting chooses the largest available entry in magnitude in the current column. In exact exam arithmetic any nonzero entry will do; the choice matters only for round-off.
The swap must be applied to the whole already-eliminated matrix, and the multipliers already sitting in the earlier columns of L must be swapped in the same way - this is the step people forget.
With partial pivoting, PA = LU exists for every square matrix, singular or not.
det(A) = det(U) / det(P), that is the product of the pivots times the sign of the permutation.

example.prompt: Factor A = [[1,2,3],[2,4,1],[4,9,2]], which needs a row exchange.
example.work: Column 1: R2 <- R2 - 2 R1 gives (0,0,-5) and R3 <- R3 - 4 R1 gives (0,1,-10). The (2,2) pivot is now 0, so swap rows 2 and 3: P is the 2-3 transposition and PA = [[1,2,3],[4,9,2],[2,4,1]]. Then R2 <- R2 - 4 R1 gives (0,1,-10) and R3 <- R3 - 2 R1 gives (0,0,-5).
example.answer: L = [[1,0,0],[4,1,0],[2,0,1]] and U = [[1,2,3],[0,1,-10],[0,0,-5]]. The product LU is PA, and since det(P) = -1 and the pivots multiply to -5, det(A) = 5.

gateAngle: Both CSE questions that print an LU factorization use matrices that need no exchange, so pivoting appears in the exam only as the background that makes the existence answer complete. It is P2 for that reason: worth one reading, because a question can always hand you a matrix with a zero in the first position and ask why the printed factorization has a P in it.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A = [[0,2],[1,3]]. Write PA = LU and give det(A).
variations.why: After the swap the matrix is already upper triangular, so the factorization is trivial; the sign of det(P) is what carries the -1, and the direct computation 0*3 - 2*1 agrees.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why must the multipliers already recorded in L be swapped along with the rows?
variations.answer: Because those multipliers describe operations applied to rows that have now changed places. If they stay put, L no longer records the operations actually performed and the product LU is not PA.
variations.why: L is a product of elementary matrices in the order they were applied; permuting rows of the working matrix permutes the corresponding factors.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A is 4x4 and its factorization required three row swaps. What is the sign in det(A) = (sign) * u11 u22 u33 u44?
variations.answer: Minus one, because three swaps is an odd number and det(P) = (-1)^3.
variations.why: Only the parity matters, so three swaps and one swap give the same sign.

trap.what: Swapping rows of A and then writing the multipliers in the order they were computed, without swapping the earlier columns of L.
trap.why: The two rows exchanged places carry their history with them, so the entries of L belonging to those rows must move too. Otherwise the recorded factors multiply to a matrix that is A with its rows in a different order, which is neither A nor PA.
trap.counterexample: In the worked example, rows 2 and 3 are exchanged after l21 = 2 and l31 = 4 have been recorded. Those two multipliers travel with their rows: after the swap the row that was third carries the multiplier 4 and becomes the second row of L, which is why L has 4 in position (2,1) and 2 in position (3,1) - the reverse of the order they were computed in.

check.question: Why can a matrix with a zero in the (1,1) position still be solved by LU, when the previous card says no unit-L factorization exists?
check.answer: Because the swap is allowed: the factorization is then PA = LU, which does exist, and you solve PA x = P b by the same two substitutions.
check.explanation: The obstruction was the zero pivot, not the matrix. Permuting the rows moves the zero out of the pivot position, and the right-hand side is permuted with the same P so the system is unchanged.

sourceLine: StatLect's LU decomposition page (English, read in part) for the PA = LU theorem, the permutation matrix as an orthogonal matrix, and the observation that the elementary matrices of elimination are lower triangular. The worked 3x3, its permutation, its factors and both determinants are recomputed in exact arithmetic in scripts/validate.py. No readable lecture this run covered pivoting, so nothing on this card is quoted from a lecture.
